## 1.Introduction

What is a function in R?

A function is a reusable block of code designed to perform a specific task. Instead of writing the same code repeatedly, you can use a function whenever you need it.

## 2.Common build in function in R

Common built-in functions in R
R has many functions that help us analyze and manipulate data.
Function	Purpose	Example
1.sum()	Calculates total	sum(c(2, 4, 6))
2.mean()	Calculates average	mean(c(2, 4, 6))
3.median()	Finds middle value	median(c(2, 4, 6))
4.max()	Finds maximum	max(c(2, 4, 6))
5.min()	Finds minimum	min(c(2, 4, 6))
6.length()	Counts elements	length(c(2, 4, 6))
7.sqrt()	Calculates square root	sqrt(25)
8.round()	Rounds numbers	round(3.456, 2)
9.sort()	Sorts values	sort(c(5, 2, 8))
10.abs()	Returns absolute value	abs(-10)


## 3.Creating my own functions

Creating a function using the function() keyword


## 4. Functions format

```{r function_format, eval=FALSE}
function_name <- function(arguments) {
  statements
  return(result)
}
```

## A. Build_in Functions


## 1. Calculate the square of a number

```{r square_func, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
square <- function(x) {
  result <- x^2
  return(result)
}
square(5)

```
## 2.Applying a function to multiple values

```{r mean_func, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
marks <- c(65, 70, 80, 85, 90)
mean(marks)

```



## 3.Maximum calculation

```{r max_func, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
marks <- c(65, 70, 80, 85, 90)
max(marks)

```


## 4.Minimum calculation

```{r min_func, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
marks <- c(65, 70, 80, 85, 90)
min(marks)

```
## 5.Sorting

```{r sort_func, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
marks <- c(65, 70, 80, 85, 90)
sort(marks)

```


## B.The user-defined functions

A user-defined function is a function that you create yourself to perform a specific task.

For example, suppose you frequently calculate the average marks of students. Instead of writing mean() every time, you can create your own function to calculate the average.

In R, we use the keyword function() to create a function.


```{r function_format, eval=FALSE}

function_name <- function(arguments) {
  statements
  return(result)
}

```


## 1. Print the result


```{r function_format, eval=FALSE}
student_marks <- c(60, 70, 80, 90, 100)

calculate_average <- function(marks) {
  average <- mean(marks)
  return(average)
}

result <- calculate_average(student_marks)

print(result)


```

## 2.Functions with multiple arguments

```{r function_format, eval=FALSE}
add_numbers <- function(a, b) {
  result <- a + b
  return(result)
}

add_numbers(20, 30)


```
## 3. Calculate the rectangul area.




```{r function_format, eval=FALSE}
rectangle_area <- function(length, width) {
  area <- length * width
  return(area)
}

rectangle_area(10, 5)


```
## 4. Functions with default argument values

R allows to assign default values to function arguments.



```{r function_format, eval=FALSE}
great_student <- function(name = "Student") {
  message <- paste("Welcome", name)
  return(message)
}

great_student()

```

```{r function_format, eval=FALSE}

great_student("Josephine")

```
## 5.Calculating discount

```{r function_format, eval=FALSE}

calculate_discount <- function(price, discount) {
  final_price <- price - discount
  return(final_price)
}

# Call the function
calculate_discount(100, 15)

```

## 5.Calculating total

```{r function_format}
total <- function(numbers) {
  final_total <- sum(numbers)
  return(final_total)
}

# Call the function
total(c(100, 15, 85))

```
